key_terms.meaning: On-demand network access to a shared, configurable pool of computing resources that can be provisioned and released with little management effort (NIST definition).
The ability to add or remove compute and storage automatically as load rises and falls, paying only for what is used.
Software that splits one physical machine into several isolated virtual machines or containers, each with its own operating system view or app.
A layer that exposes sensors owned by many different providers as virtual sensors that any application can request, combine and release on demand.
The cloud-side list that stores each device's unique ID, credentials, type and metadata, and decides which devices may connect.
A publish/subscribe server that receives messages on topics from devices and forwards them to every subscriber of that topic.
A JSON document in the cloud holding a device's last reported state and its desired state, readable even when the device is offline.
A cloud service that watches incoming device messages and triggers actions such as a database write, an alert or a command to another device.
Analytics that runs on each message as it arrives, in order, with low delay, instead of storing everything first.
Grouping an endless stream into finite chunks by time or count, for example tumbling windows of 1 minute or sliding windows of 5 minutes every 1 minute.
A handshake in which the device proves its identity to the cloud and the cloud proves its identity to the device, usually with X.509 certificates.
The encryption protocol that protects IoT data in transit between device, gateway and cloud, giving confidentiality and integrity.
Giving permissions to roles such as viewer, operator or admin, then assigning users and services to roles instead of to individual rights.
Removing or generalizing identifiers such as name, address and exact timestamp so stored data cannot be tied back to a person.
A design that exposes each device as a web resource with a URL, a standard API and a machine-readable description.
A standard document listing a device's properties, actions, events and the protocol bindings an application can use to reach it.
A software layer between devices and applications that hides protocol and hardware differences and offers common services such as routing, filtering and device management.
A network design where a central controller computes forwarding decisions and installs them into simple switches, separating control from forwarding.
The elected node in a cluster that collects data from member nodes, aggregates it and forwards it to the gateway or cloud.
Keeping copies of the same data at gateway and cloud consistent by exchanging updates, versions or timestamps and resolving conflicts.

takeaways: Cloud computing gives IoT an elastic shared pool of compute, storage and services, so you do not size a server for peak load forever.
A sensor cloud turns many owners' physical sensors into virtual sensors that applications can request, combine and release on demand.
An IoT cloud platform replaces your custom server with four built-in functions: device identity, a message broker, a rules engine and managed storage.
MQTT with topics and a device shadow lets thousands of constrained devices publish small messages and survive going offline.
IoT analytics mixes stream processing for alerts with batch storage for history, and windowing makes an endless stream computable.
Security covers device identity, data in transit, data at rest and access control; privacy decides what personal data you collect at all.
The Web of Things exposes devices as described web resources, while middleware hides protocol differences from the application.
SDN moves routing decisions into a central controller, which suits dynamic IoT traffic but creates a single point of failure to design around.
Clustering, agents and synchronization keep large IoT deployments scalable by deciding locally and reconciling copies later.
Agent-based local decisions plus eventual consistency usually beat a strict central lock for a sensor network spread over a city.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to define the concept, draw the layered architecture or flow, list its components with one line each, and finish with an IoT example plus the limitation.

bank.q: Define cloud computing as given by NIST. List its essential characteristics and explain how each one helps an IoT deployment.
outline: NIST definition: on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable resources, rapidly provisioned and released
On-demand self-service: a team starts a broker without raising a purchase order
Broad network access: devices reach services over standard IP
Resource pooling: many devices share servers through multi-tenancy
Rapid elasticity: scale up at morning peak, scale down at night
Measured service: pay per message or per GB-hour
IoT example: 10,000 smart meters sending readings every 15 minutes

bank.q: Explain the sensor cloud concept. What are virtual sensors, who owns the physical sensors, and what benefit does an application get?
outline: Physical sensors owned by different providers, each with its own interface
Virtual sensor: a logical sensor created on request with the chosen location, sampling rate and duration
Sensor cloud layer does discovery, selection, composition and data delivery
Application does not buy or maintain hardware; it rents sensing
Benefits: cost sharing, coverage of many locations, reuse of existing deployments
Issues: trust in data quality, privacy of the sensing region, availability

bank.q: Describe the four core functions that an IoT cloud platform provides. Illustrate with AWS IoT or Azure IoT Hub.
outline: Device identity and registry: unique device ID plus credentials
Message broker over MQTT or HTTPS with topics or per-device endpoints
Rules engine: SQL-like queries on incoming messages triggering actions
Managed storage plus integration with databases, queues and dashboards
Security services: certificates, policies, per-device permissions
Device management: firmware update, configuration, monitoring
Mention the shadow or twin for offline devices

bank.q: Compare stream processing and batch processing for IoT data. Explain windowing with a tumbling and a sliding example.
outline: Batch: store first, process later on large files; high throughput, high latency
Stream: process each event on arrival; low latency, bounded memory
IoT needs both: alerts in seconds, reports and models over months
Windowing groups an endless stream into finite sets
Tumbling window: fixed, non-overlapping, for example 1 minute averages
Sliding window: overlapping, for example 5-minute average computed every 1 minute
Session window: gap-based, useful for activity bursts
State and late-arriving data must be handled

bank.q: Define software defined networking. Distinguish the control plane from the data plane and explain how a controller programs a switch.
outline: SDN separates the control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding)
Switch keeps only flow tables; controller computes routes and policies
Southbound API such as OpenFlow installs match-action rules
Northbound API lets applications request policies
Central view of the whole network simplifies policy change
Benefits: programmability, slicing, central security policy
Risks: controller is a single point of failure, needs protection and replication

bank.q: Differentiate the Web of Things from IoT middleware, and state one situation where each is the better choice.
outline: WoT: devices exposed as web resources with URLs, REST verbs and a Thing Description
WoT standardizes the interface so any web client can interact
Middleware: a software layer that hides protocols and hardware below the application
Middleware services: protocol translation, routing, filtering, caching, device management
WoT when third parties must discover and use devices across vendors
Middleware when many legacy protocols must be unified inside one product

bank.q: A factory has 500 temperature sensors. Each sends one 200-byte reading every 10 seconds. Size the cloud side: messages per second, data per day, and choose a broker plus storage strategy for live alerts and one-year history.
outline: Messages per second = 500 / 10 = 50 messages/s
Bytes per second = 50 x 200 = 10,000 B/s = 10 kB/s
Per day = 10 kB/s x 86,400 s = 864,000 kB, about 864 MB/day
Per year about 315 GB before replication and indexing
Broker: MQTT with QoS level suited to alerting; one topic per machine or per sensor type
Hot path: stream processing with a 1-minute tumbling window for threshold alerts
Cold path: write raw to object storage or a time-series database, downsample older data
Add retention policy, compression and partitioning by device ID

bank.q: You must provision and protect a fleet of 5,000 electricity smart meters that connect to a cloud platform. Describe the security steps from manufacturing to daily operation.
outline: Unique device identity per meter, certificate or key injected at manufacture
Register each device in the cloud registry, mark it as provisioned
Mutual authentication with TLS so a fake server cannot collect readings
Per-device policy: the meter may publish only to its own topic
RBAC for human users: installer, operator, auditor
Key rotation and revocation for stolen or retired meters
Firmware update signed and verified, staged rollout
Data at rest encrypted; billing data access logged
Fallback: quarantine a device that behaves abnormally

bank.q: A campus has 2,000 sensor nodes sending readings to one gateway. Apply clustering to reduce traffic and compute the reduction if clusters of 20 nodes each send one aggregated message per round instead of every node sending one.
outline: Cluster head election by residual energy, distance and rotation
Members send to the head over short hops; the head aggregates and forwards
Number of clusters = 2000 / 20 = 100
Messages reaching the gateway per round fall from 2000 to 100, a 20x reduction
Energy saved on long-range radio at the members
Costs: aggregation delay, head energy drain, need for rotation
State that cluster heads forward summaries, so raw data is lost unless sampled

bank.q: A building has legacy Modbus sensors. Show how you would expose them through the Web of Things so a web dashboard can read them without knowing Modbus.
outline: Gateway reads Modbus registers on a polling cycle
Map each register to a WoT property with a name, type and unit
Write a Thing Description listing properties, events and a protocol binding
Gateway offers HTTP or MQTT binding with JSON payloads
Dashboard uses the description to build its view automatically
Security: authenticate the dashboard, allow read-only access
State the mapping table as the single place to change when a sensor is added

bank.q: Compare AWS IoT and Azure IoT Hub on device identity, protocol support, rules and device state. Recommend one for a start-up with 300 devices and justify.
outline: Both: per-device identity, certificate based mutual TLS, MQTT and HTTPS support
AWS IoT Core: policies attached to certificates, rules engine with SQL-like statements, device shadow
Azure IoT Hub: per-device SAS tokens or certificates, routes and endpoints, device twin with desired and reported properties, built-in device management
Compare pricing units: connectivity plus messages versus tiered message allowance per day
Compare ecosystem lock-in, tooling maturity, regional availability
Recommendation must state a criterion such as cost at 300 devices, team skills, existing cloud use
Close with the migration risk of proprietary features

bank.q: A home security product uploads continuous video and door-sensor logs to the cloud. Analyse the privacy risks and propose design changes using data minimization, retention limits and anonymization.
outline: Identify personal data: faces, voices, occupancy pattern, timestamps
Risks: pattern-of-life inference, unauthorized sharing, breach impact, over-retention
Minimization: record only on motion or door-open events, drop audio if not needed
On-device processing to send events and labels instead of raw video
Retention: keep short rolling window, delete after N days unless flagged
Anonymization: blur faces, generalize timestamps for analytics copies
Access control and audit logs for who watched what
Consent and a clear notice to household members and visitors
Trade-off: less data reduces both privacy risk and model quality

bank.q: Evaluate whether software defined networking is justified for a city-wide IoT network. Discuss benefits, controller failure, latency and scalability.
outline: Benefits: central policy for thousands of devices, network slicing per application, fast reconfiguration
Traffic engineering for bursty sensor uploads
Controller placement: local controllers per zone, replicated for failure
Failure analysis: if the controller is down, switches keep last rules, so degrade gracefully not stop
Latency of control messages versus data path; keep data plane local
Scalability: flow table size, controller throughput, east-west consistency
Security: the controller is a high-value target, secure channel needed
Verdict: justified when policy changes are frequent and devices many, overkill for a small fixed deployment

bank.q: In a sensor cloud, several tenants share physical sensors while gateways cache data locally. Analyse how multi-tenancy and data synchronization interact, and evaluate a suitable consistency choice.
outline: Multi-tenancy: one physical sensor serves several virtual sensors with different rates and privacy rules
Isolation must hold for data and for query load
Gateways cache during network loss, so copies diverge
Synchronization options: version vectors, timestamps, last-writer-wins, per-tenant logs
Last-writer-wins loses data when sensors emit different readings; per-reading append logs avoid loss
Strong consistency costs availability during a Chennai power cut or link loss
Eventual consistency fits sensor readings if the application tolerates a short delay
Evaluate: choose eventual consistency plus conflict-free append per tenant, reserving strong consistency for billing or alarms

glossary.def: Delivery of computing, storage and services over a network from a shared pool, provisioned on demand.
A software-defined computer with its own operating system running on shared physical hardware.
A lightweight isolated package of an application and its libraries that shares the host operating system kernel.
Automatic addition or removal of resources as demand changes.
One physical system serving several customers with logical isolation between their data and workloads.
A platform that virtualizes sensors from many owners so applications can request sensing as a service.
A logical sensor created on demand from one or more physical sensors with chosen location, rate and duration.
A managed service offering device identity, a message broker, rules, storage and device management for connected devices.
A server that receives published messages and forwards them to subscribers, decoupling senders from receivers.
A named string in a publish/subscribe system, such as home/room1/temperature, that subscribers match against.
A delivery guarantee level: at most once, at least once, or exactly once.
A cloud copy of a device's reported and desired state, usable while the device is offline.
A service that evaluates conditions on incoming messages and triggers actions when they match.
Continuous computation on events as they arrive, with low latency.
Computation over a stored, bounded collection of data, usually with high throughput and higher latency.
A finite grouping of stream events by time or count so that aggregates can be computed.
A store that keeps raw data in its native format until it is needed for analysis.
A model of a physical asset kept in step with its live data and used for simulation and prediction.
Proving that a device or user is who it claims to be.
Deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to do.
A signed digital document binding a public key to a device or server identity.
Storing data in encrypted form so a stolen disk or backup does not reveal it.
Collecting only the data actually needed for a stated purpose.
Exposing devices as described web resources reachable over standard web protocols.
A machine-readable document describing a device's properties, actions, events and protocol bindings.
Software between devices and applications that hides protocol and hardware differences.
A network architecture with a centralized controller that installs forwarding rules into switches.
A switch table of match fields and actions that tells the switch how to handle each packet.
Grouping nodes so a chosen head aggregates their data and reduces long-range traffic.
The node that collects, aggregates and forwards data for its cluster.
A program that moves between nodes and runs locally, carrying code instead of shipping raw data.
The process of making copies of data on different nodes agree.
A guarantee that replicas will converge to the same value if no new updates occur.
